title: Builder Pattern
summary: Constructing complex, valid objects step by step — chaining named calls and validating once at the end — instead of telescoping constructors.

slides.markdown: **Builder** solves a different problem than the other patterns in this group: not *which* class to instantiate, but how to construct *one* complex object step by step when it has many optional parts. Instead of a constructor with nine parameters, you chain calls — `.setHost(...).setTimeout(...).build()` — and validate everything once, at the end. Think of ordering a custom sandwich: you pick ingredients one at a time, and the sandwich isn't "built" until you say so.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: telescoping constructors with many optional parameters
Builder: construct step by step, validate at the end
slides.markdown:
**Builder** separates *setting* values from *validating and assembling* them: you call one method per optional field, in any order, and a final `build()` call checks everything together and produces the finished object.

```java
HttpRequest req = new HttpRequestBuilder()
    .url("https://api.example.com")
    .timeout(5000)
    .header("Authorization", token)
    .build();
```

Each call is self-documenting — `.timeout(5000)` tells you exactly what's being set, unlike a bare `5000` in a constructor call. `build()` is also the natural place to enforce invariants that span multiple fields, like "retries requires a timeout to be set."

Takeaway: Builder trades one big constructor call for several small, named ones plus a single validation point.

![Director calling Builder which produces a Product](assets/builder-roles.svg)

Builder has three possible roles: the **product** (the object being assembled), the **builder** (accumulates state and validates), and an optional **director** (calls the builder's steps in a fixed, reusable sequence).

Most modern code skips the director and calls builder methods directly from application code — it's useful mainly when the *same* build sequence needs to run in multiple places with different builders.

assets.alt: Director calling Builder which produces a Product

slides.sectionTitle: Fluent builders vs a separate director object
slides.markdown:
A **fluent builder** returns `this` from every setter so calls chain: `.timeout(5000).retries(3).build()`. It's the dominant style today because most callers just want to set a few fields once, inline, with no reuse of the sequence itself.

A **director** object is worth adding only when the *same sequence of builder calls* needs to run from multiple places — for example, a `StandardRequestDirector` that always sets a default timeout and a tracing header, so every caller gets those two fields for free without repeating the calls.

Most interview-level Builder implementations skip the director entirely; mention it to show you know it exists, but don't over-engineer a simple case with one.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: building an immutable HttpRequest via chained builder calls
Compare: Builder vs constructor overloading vs named-parameter languages
slides.markdown:
How three approaches solve "many optional constructor parameters," ranked by what each buys you.

| | Readability at call site | Validates as a whole | Needs extra boilerplate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Constructor overloading | Poor — positional args, easy to swap | Only inside each overload | No |
| Builder | Good — named, chainable calls | Yes, in `build()` | Yes — a builder class |
| Named parameters (Python, Kotlin) | Good — `HttpRequest(url=..., timeout=...)` | Only inside the constructor | No |

**How to decide:** if your language has real named/default parameters, use them first — Builder's extra class solves a problem those languages don't have. Reach for Builder in Java/C++-style languages, or when you need multi-field validation a single constructor call can't cleanly express.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a builder that allows building an invalid or half-configured object
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "As long as I have a builder, the object it produces is safe."

**Why it's wrong:** a builder only helps if `build()` actually validates. A builder that just copies whatever fields were set — including none of them — into the product will happily hand back a half-configured `HttpRequest` with a null URL, which then fails somewhere far from where it was actually misconfigured.

**Correct model:** `build()` must check every invariant the product needs — required fields present, cross-field rules satisfied, like "retries implies a timeout" — and throw immediately if they're violated. The whole point of centralizing construction is centralizing validation too; skipping that turns Builder into telescoping constructors with extra steps.

slides.sectionTitle: Where Builder pairs with immutability for thread-safe objects
slides.markdown:
Builder and immutability are a natural pair: the builder absorbs all the mutation — setters, partial state, edits while configuring — and the product it returns is a plain immutable object: final fields, no setters, safe to hand to any thread without synchronization.

This matters because an immutable object can be freely shared and cached: once `build()` returns, nothing can change its state out from under a concurrent reader, so you don't need locks just to read a request's timeout value.

The practical pattern: keep all mutability inside the builder, and make the built object as immutable as the domain allows — the harder problem of coordinating concurrent *mutation* simply doesn't arise for something that can't be mutated.
